newsitem.title: USA: Stocks fall on fears of higher interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Stocks fall on fears of higher interest rates.

text.p: Stocks fell sharply along with bonds Thursday after the release of robust retail sales data revived fears the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates later this month.

At 1 p.m. EST, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 75.43 points at 6,963.94. In the broader market, declines led advances by 8 to 3 on active New York Stock Exchange volume of 260 million shares
Trading curbs were put in place on the NYSE just 12 minutes after the opening when the Dow lost more than 50 points.
"Retail sales kicked off the decline today," said Joseph Barthel, chief investment strategist at Fahnestock & Co.
"Everyone is really anxious over the coming meeting of the FOMC," Barthel said, referring to the Federal Open Market Committee, the Fed's policy-making arm, which meets March 25.
Barthel said Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has indicated that he would like to raise interest rates if the economy showed more signs of strength.
"And lo and behold, we get data this morning which implies that the consumer is not tapped out and that there is still some strength in the economy," Barthel said.

The Commerce Department reported that total retail sales increased 0.8 percent last month after a sharply revised 1.5 percent jump in January -- more than double the previously reported 0.6 percent pickup in January sales.
The revised January sales increase was the strongest monthly gain since February last year, when sales soared by 1.9 percent.

The strong retail sales numbers sent the inflation-sensitive 30-year Treasury bond down nearly three-quarters of a point, sending its yield up to 6.94 percent from 6.88 percent on Wednesday. The bond price and yield move in opposite directions.
Jobless claims for the week ended March 8 rose by a lower-than-forecast 307,000, compared with an upwardly revised 312,000 a year ago, the Labour Department said.
Barthel said, however, he believed that Greenspan was in a bind and that he would not be able to hike rates.

"There is a big difference between perception and reality," Barthel said. "He is in a bind. There is not enough cumulative evidence that the economy is really percolating, there is almost no inflation and growth is moderate."

Semiconductor companies, computer disk drive makers and networking firms were bright spots amid the overall decline on Thursday, gaining ground after several analysts raised their ratings on key stocks.

Disk makers Quantum Corp., up 1-1/4 at 40-3/4, and Western Digital Corp., up 7/8 at 65-3/8, were upgraded by Smith Barney. Shares in electronics maker Analogue Devices Inc. rose 1/4 to 23-3/8. UBS Securities raised the stock to "buy."
Cisco Systems Inc., the most active Nasdaq issue, was up 1-1/4 at 52-1/8, Oracle Corp. rose 1 to 35-1/8. Intel Corp., however, fell 1-7/8 to 140-7/8.
The Nasdaq index was off 4.54 points at 1,299.59. The Standard & Poors index of 500 stocks was down 7.50 at 796.76.
The American Stock Exchange index was off 1.99 points at 600.05.
